entries.name: Rejection sampling
entries.definition: A random-variate generation algorithm that draws proposals from a normalized envelope dominating an unnormalized target and accepts each with the target-to-envelope ratio, yielding independent target draws with fresh independent random trials.
entries.identity_notes: This is ordinary accept-reject generation with a valid global envelope. A rejected candidate is discarded, not recorded as a repeated chain state. The method differs from Metropolis acceptance, rejection-driven Metropolis proposals, importance weighting and selective filtering of model answers. The inspected primary source presents the scalar density case.
entries.mechanism: For a nonnegative target g with finite positive integral, choose an integrable envelope g_u with g_u(x)≥g(x) everywhere on the target support and sample x from g_u/integral(g_u). Independently draw w uniformly on (0,1); accept x if w≤g(x)/g_u(x), otherwise discard the trial and repeat. An optional lower bound 0≤g_l≤g allows early acceptance when the same w≤g_l(x)/g_u(x), avoiding evaluation of g. Fresh independent trials produce independent accepted draws from normalized g. The target normalizing constant is not required for the acceptance ratio.
entries.locator: Section 2.1, Rejection Sampling, printed pp. 338–339 / PDF pp. 3–4
limitations: A valid dominating envelope and an exact sampler for its normalized distribution are required. Clipping an invalid envelope ratio at one does not preserve the intended independent-sample law.
An envelope with excessive mass can make acceptance rare. No universal efficiency, dimensional scaling or bound on the number of trials is claimed.
The optional squeezing bound must be valid everywhere it is used; it is an evaluation shortcut, not a replacement target.
Numerical approximation, finite precision and inaccurate envelope sampling can change the output distribution. Log concavity is not required by ordinary rejection sampling itself.

entries.name: Adaptive rejection sampling
entries.definition: The Gilks–Wild univariate rejection sampler that uses tangents to a concave log density as a piecewise-linear upper hull and chords as a lower hull, updating these bounds from evaluated proposals.
entries.identity_notes: This record scopes ARS to the derivative-based tangent construction in Gilks and Wild (1992), for a fixed log-concave scalar target on a connected domain. Derivative-free envelope constructions and adaptive rejection Metropolis sampling are distinct variants requiring their own evidence. Exact conditional draws do not make successive joint Gibbs states independent.
entries.mechanism: Write h=log g for a differentiable concave log density. At ordered support points evaluate h and h prime; tangent intersections define an upper hull u, and chords define a lower hull l, with l=−infinity outside the extreme support points. Initialize points so exp(u) is integrable; on unbounded tails this requires a positive leftmost slope and a negative rightmost slope. Draw x from normalized exp(u) and w uniformly on (0,1). Accept immediately if w≤exp(l(x)−u(x)); otherwise evaluate h(x) and h prime(x), accept if w≤exp(h(x)−u(x)), and incorporate the evaluated point into the hulls whether that full test accepted or rejected it. Repeat rejected trials. The conditional-on-history rejection argument gives the fixed target law for each output despite adaptation of the valid bounds.
entries.locator: Sections 2.2–2.3, Equations (1)–(4), initialization, sampling step and correctness argument, printed pp. 339–342 / PDF pp. 4–7; conclusion on numerical care, p. 347 / PDF p. 12
limitations: Concavity of log g is essential for the tangent and chord bounds. Unimodality alone is insufficient, and non-log-concave targets are not covered by this construction.
The displayed baseline assumes usable derivatives and connected scalar support. It does not assert validity for every nonsmooth density or a direct multivariate joint draw.
Tail slopes and support endpoints must make the proposal integrable. Concentrated or skewed densities require numerical care.
When a Gibbs conditional changes, hull values must be computed for that conditional; reusing stale density bounds is not justified.
No universal evaluation savings or benchmark result is asserted. ARMS and its 1997 correction remain separate uninspected-method leads.

entries.name: Elliptical slice sampling
entries.definition: A Markov-chain update for a target factored into a Gaussian prior and a likelihood, which performs an angular slice search along the ellipse defined by the current state and an independent prior draw.
entries.identity_notes: This is the full-circle default algorithm in Murray et al. Figure 2 for a fixed Gaussian prior covariance. It differs from a fixed-angle Gaussian autoregressive Metropolis proposal and from scalar interval stepping-out or doubling. ESS here denotes this sampler, not the effective-sample-size diagnostic.
entries.mechanism: For pi(f) proportional to Normal(f;0,Sigma)L(f), draw nu from Normal(0,Sigma), then log y=log L(f)+log u for independent u uniform on (0,1). Draw theta uniformly on (0,2pi) and initialize [theta_min,theta_max]=[theta−2pi,theta]. Test f_prime=f cos(theta)+nu sin(theta); accept when log L(f_prime)>log y. Otherwise shrink the bracket at theta on the side determined by its sign relative to zero, redraw theta uniformly from that bracket, and repeat with the same nu, f and threshold. The randomly positioned bracket retains the angle zero corresponding to the current state. Gaussian rotational invariance and the reversible bracket construction give the target-invariant transition.
entries.locator: Sections 2.1–2.3, Figure 2 and correctness proof, printed pp. 542–545 / PDF pp. 2–5
limitations: A Gaussian prior draw and likelihood evaluation are required. A nonzero prior mean must be handled by centering the ellipse; an arbitrary non-Gaussian prior is outside this formula.
Fixing the initial bracket deterministically to [−pi,pi] is not the proved algorithm; the paper explicitly explains why its random placement matters.

The algorithm may reject multiple internal angle trials before returning an update. Its lack of an outer Metropolis rejection is not a claim of one likelihood evaluation or independent retained states.
The default full-circle algorithm avoids a user-specified proposal scale, but covariance, model hyperparameters and optional narrower angular variants still involve choices.
Strong offsets, covariance structure and likelihood geometry can impede exploration. No universal mixing rate, finite-run accuracy or timing advantage is asserted.

entries.name: Rejection-driven independence Metropolis sampling
entries.definition: An independence Metropolis sampler whose proposals are generated by a rejection procedure with a fixed possibly non-dominating envelope, followed by a Metropolis correction for the resulting clipped proposal law.
entries.identity_notes: This is Tierney’s rejection sampling chain in Section 2.3.4. It specializes independence Metropolis by an inner proposal generator; it is not ordinary rejection sampling unless the envelope dominates everywhere. It is distinct from adaptive rejection Metropolis sampling, because h and c are fixed here.
entries.mechanism: For a proper target pi and a normalized proposal density h covering its support, fix c>0. Repeatedly draw z from h and u uniformly on (0,c h(z)) until u<pi(z). This yields a proposal y with density f proportional to min(pi,c h). At current state x apply independence Metropolis acceptance min(1,pi(y)f(x)/(pi(x)f(y))); retain x if rejected. Let C={x:pi(x)≤c h(x)}. The published acceptance cases are 1 when x is in C; c h(x)/pi(x) when x is outside C and y is in C; and min(1,pi(y)h(x)/(pi(x)h(y))) when both are outside C. Normalizing constants of f cancel. When c h dominates pi everywhere, this reduces to independent rejection sampling.
entries.locator: Sections 2.3.1, 2.3.3–2.3.4, especially Rejection sampling chains, printed pp. 1704–1707 / PDF pp. 5–8
limitations: The inner proposal must have positive acceptance mass and cover the target support required for irreducibility. A poor choice of h or c can make either stage inefficient.
The inner rejected trials are discarded, while rejection by the outer Metropolis test repeats the chain state; these two rejection events have different roles.
A non-dominating envelope without the outer correction generally gives the clipped density rather than pi. Correcting it does not guarantee fast mixing.

The inspected 1991 technical report prints the reciprocal of the mixed-case factor and omits the minimum with one in the final case. This record uses the visually verified 1994 published expressions, consistent with the general independence ratio; no separate erratum is asserted.
Adapting h or c from chain history is outside the fixed-proposal definition and needs its own validity argument.

entries.name: Crank–Nicolson Metropolis sampling
entries.definition: A Metropolis sampler for a Gaussian-reference target using a Crank–Nicolson discretization of the unpreconditioned reference Ornstein–Uhlenbeck dynamics as its proposal.
entries.identity_notes: This is the CN proposal of Cotter et al. Section 4.2 paired with its Metropolis test, not the generic Crank–Nicolson numerical integration scheme. Unlike pCN, its proposal requires an operator or matrix solve involving C and the step size. It contains no likelihood-gradient drift.
entries.mechanism: For finite-dimensional pi(u) proportional to exp(−Phi(u)) Normal(u;0,C), with fixed symmetric positive-definite C, choose delta>0 and draw w from Normal(0,C). Solve (2C+delta I)v=(2C−delta I)u+sqrt(8 delta C)w, where the square root is the symmetric matrix square root. Accept v with min(1,exp(Phi(u)−Phi(v))); otherwise retain u. Equivalently, with L=C inverse, (I+delta L/2)v=(I−delta L/2)u+sqrt(2 delta)xi for standard Gaussian xi. The proposal is reversible with respect to the Gaussian reference, so the Gaussian factors cancel in Metropolis acceptance even though the proposal need not be symmetric in Euclidean coordinates.
limitations: The target must be proper relative to the Gaussian reference. The explicit density-ratio implementation here is finite-dimensional with symmetric positive-definite C; function-space extensions require the source’s operator, regularity and absolute-continuity assumptions.
Target invariance does not imply independent draws, good exploration or finite-run accuracy. Mesh-robust behavior under stated assumptions is not a universal dimension-free performance guarantee.
C and the step size are fixed in the stated kernel. Adaptive covariance or step-size policies need separate validity arguments.

The reprint’s later Equation (6.2) reverses signs relative to Equation (6.1) and the explicit Section 4 proposals. This record uses Section 4 and does not claim a published erratum or use the inconsistent expression.
An accurate linear solve and Gaussian draw are required. Replacing the noise by an incorrectly scaled standard Gaussian changes the proposal and invalidates the stated cancellation.

entries.name: Preconditioned Crank–Nicolson sampling
entries.definition: A Metropolis sampler for a Gaussian-reference target whose proposal combines the current state with an independent draw from that reference using a scalar autoregressive coefficient.
entries.identity_notes: This is the pCN proposal and likelihood-ratio test in Cotter et al. Section 4.2. It preserves the Gaussian reference before correction and differs from an additive random walk, the unpreconditioned CN solve and an angular slice search. The displayed nonnegative coefficient form uses the source’s delta≤2 parameterization.
entries.mechanism: For finite-dimensional pi(u) proportional to exp(−Phi(u)) Normal(u;0,C), with fixed symmetric positive-definite C, choose 0<beta≤1, draw w from Normal(0,C), and set v=sqrt(1−beta squared)u+beta w. Accept with min(1,exp(Phi(u)−Phi(v))); otherwise retain u. For 0<delta≤2 this equals (2+delta)v=(2−delta)u+sqrt(8 delta)w with beta squared=8 delta/(2+delta) squared. Gaussian-reference reversibility cancels the prior and proposal factors in the full Metropolis ratio. At beta=1 the proposal is an independent prior draw, while the retained states can still be correlated through rejection.
entries.locator: Introduction Equation (1.1) and algorithm, Section 4.2 Equations (4.7)–(4.11), reprint/PDF pp. 3 and 10–11
limitations: The target must be proper relative to the Gaussian reference. The explicit density-ratio implementation here is finite-dimensional with symmetric positive-definite C; function-space extensions require the source’s operator, regularity and absolute-continuity assumptions.
Target invariance does not imply independent draws, good exploration or finite-run accuracy. Mesh-robust behavior under stated assumptions is not a universal dimension-free performance guarantee.

The reprint’s later Equation (6.2) reverses signs relative to Equation (6.1) and the explicit Section 4 proposals. This record uses Section 4 and does not claim a published erratum or use the inconsistent expression.

entries.name: Crank–Nicolson Langevin sampling
entries.definition: A Metropolis-corrected Gaussian-reference sampler that combines a Crank–Nicolson treatment of the reference precision with an explicit gradient drift of the remaining target potential.
entries.identity_notes: This is Cotter et al. CNL, with unpreconditioned dynamics and a precision-dependent linear solve. The potential gradient is of Phi relative to the Gaussian reference, not of the entire Lebesgue log density. It differs from CN by its gradient term and from pCNL by its preconditioning.
entries.mechanism: For finite-dimensional pi(u) proportional to exp(−Phi(u)) Normal(u;0,C), with fixed symmetric positive-definite C, assume differentiable Phi, choose delta>0 and draw w from Normal(0,C). Solve (2C+delta I)v=(2C−delta I)u−2 delta C grad Phi(u)+sqrt(8 delta C)w. Let q(v|u) be this Gaussian proposal. In finite dimensions accept with min(1,pi(v)q(u|v)/(pi(u)q(v|u))) and otherwise retain u, evaluating the reverse proposal at v. This is the ordinary-density specialization of the source’s general Metropolis construction and its rho-based CNL acceptance. The gradient changes proposal reversibility, so the CN likelihood-only ratio cannot simply be reused.

entries.name: Preconditioned Crank–Nicolson Langevin sampling
entries.definition: A Metropolis-corrected Gaussian-reference sampler that preconditions the potential-gradient drift by the reference covariance and uses a scalar Crank–Nicolson autoregressive update.
entries.identity_notes: This is Cotter et al. pCNL. The reference covariance multiplies grad Phi, and the linear denominator is the scalar 2+delta, distinguishing it from the CNL matrix solve. Set v=((2−delta)u−2 delta C grad Phi(u)+sqrt(8 delta)w)/(2+delta). Its Gaussian covariance is 8 delta C/(2+delta) squared. Let q be that proposal; accept with min(1,pi(v)q(u|v)/(pi(u)q(v|u))) and otherwise retain u, using the reverse gradient-dependent mean at v. This finite-dimensional expression specializes the source’s general Metropolis rule and pCNL rho acceptance. The prior-cancelled pCN likelihood ratio alone is generally insufficient for this gradient-directed kernel.
